q: 1. The point, through which the whole weight of the body acts, irrespective of its position, is known as
explain: The Centre of Gravity (CG) is the theoretical point where the entire weight of a body is concentrated. For a body in a uniform gravitational field, this coincides with the center of mass.

q: 2. The term 'centroid' is
options: the same as centre of gravity
the point of application of the resultant of all the forces tending to cause a body to rotate about a certain axis
explain: In engineering mechanics, for a thin plate or a plane figure of uniform thickness and density, the centroid of the area is mathematically identical to the centre of gravity.

q: 3. The centre of gravity of an equilateral triangle with each side a, is ________ form any of the three sides.
explain: The CG of a triangle lies at a height of h/3 from the base. For an equilateral triangle, the height h = (√3/2)a. Therefore, CG = (1/3) * (√3/2)a = a / (2√3).

q: 4. The centre of gravity of a semi-circle lies at a distance of ________ from its base measured along the vertical radius.
explain: For a solid semi-circle, the centroidal distance from the base diameter along the axis of symmetry is given by the formula 4r / 3π.

q: 5. The centre of gravity of a trapezium with parallel sides a and b lies at a distance of y from the base b. The value of y is
explain: The vertical distance of the centroid of a trapezium from base 'b' is calculated as (h/3) * ((2a + b) / (a + b)).

q: 6. The centre of gravity of a right circular solid cone is at a distance of ________ from its base, measured along the vertical axis.
explain: For a solid cone, the center of gravity lies on the vertical axis at a distance of 1/4th of the total height (h/4) from the base.

q: 7. The moment of inertia of a square of side (a) about an axis through its centre of gravity is
explain: Using the formula for a rectangle (bd³/12), where b=a and d=a, the MI of a square is (a * a³) / 12 = a^4 / 12.

q: 8. The moment of inertia of a rectangular section 3 cm wide and 4 cm deep about X-X axis is
9. Moment of inertia of a circular section about its diameter (d) is
explain: The standard formula for the area moment of inertia of a circle about its centroidal axis (diameter) is πd⁴ / 64.

q: 10. Moment of inertia of a circular section about an axis perpendicular to the section is
explain: This refers to the Polar Moment of Inertia (J). According to the perpendicular axis theorem, J = Ixx + Iyy = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32.

q: 11. The C.G. of a solid right circular cone lies on the axis at a height
options: half of the total height above the base
one-third of the total height above the base
one-fourth of the total height above the base
explain: As established in Q6, the CG of a solid cone is located at h/4 from the base.

q: 12. The C.G. of a thin hollow right circular cone lies on the axis at a height
explain: For a thin hollow cone (surface area only), the CG lies at a height of h/3 from the base along the vertical axis.

q: 13. The C.G. of a semi-circular arc is at the central radius at a distance of
explain: For a wire bent into a semi-circular arc (line element), the CG is located at 2r/π from the diameter.

q: 14. The C.G. of a quadrant of a circle is at a distance of
explain: The CG of a quarter circle is symmetric and located at a distance of 4r/3π from both bounding radii (axes).

q: 15. The C.G. of a thin hollow hemisphere is at a distance of
explain: The CG of a hollow hemispherical shell lies exactly at the midpoint of the central radius, which is r/2 from the base.

q: 16. The C.G. of a solid cone lies on the central axis at a distance of
options: 1/3 of the total height above base
half the total height above base
1/4 of the total height above base
2/5 of the total height above base
explain: Repeated concept: Solid cone CG is at h/4 from the base.

q: 17. The C.G. of a hollow cone lies on the central axis above base at a distance of
explain: Repeated concept: Hollow cone CG is at h/3 from the base.

q: 18. The C.G. of a hollow pyramid lies on the central axis above base at a distance of
explain: Similar to a hollow cone, a hollow pyramid (surface area) has its CG at h/3 from the base.

q: 19. The C.G. of a hollow cylinder lies on the vertical axis above base at a distance of
explain: Due to symmetry, the CG of any cylinder (solid or hollow) lies at the geometric center, which is h/2 from the base.

q: 20. If Ix = M.O.I. about x-axis and Iy = M.O.I. about y-axis, then moment of inertia about z-axis is given by
explain: This is the Perpendicular Axis Theorem, applicable to planar bodies where the Z-axis is perpendicular to the X-Y plane.

q: 22. Moment of inertia of a rectangular section having b = Width and d = Depth about x-axis is given by
explain: The standard formula for MI of a rectangle about its centroidal X-X axis (parallel to width b) is bd³/12.

q: 23. M.O.I. of a circular section of diameter d about an axis passing through its C.G. lying in the plane of the section is given by
explain: The Moment of Inertia of a circle about its diameter is πd⁴/64.

q: 24. M.O.I. of a triangular section about an axis passing through its base is given by
explain: While the MI about the centroidal axis is bh³/36, using the parallel axis theorem, the MI about the base is bh³/12.

q: 25. M.O.I. of a triangular section, about and axis passing through its C.G. is
explain: The standard formula for the moment of inertia of a triangle about its centroidal axis parallel to the base is bh³/36.

q: 26. M.O.I. of a solid sphere of mass M and radius R is given by
explain: The mass moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about any diameter is (2/5)MR².

q: 27. M.O.I. of a thin spherical shell of mass M and radius r is given as
explain: The mass moment of inertia of a thin hollow spherical shell about any diameter is (2/3)Mr².

q: 28. M.O.I. of a solid cone about its vertical axis is
explain: The mass moment of inertia of a solid right circular cone about its longitudinal (vertical) axis is (3/10)Mr².

q: 29. The units of moment of inertia of mass are
explain: Mass Moment of Inertia is defined as Σmr², so the unit is mass (kg) times distance squared (m²).

q: 30. The units of moment of inertia of area are
explain: Area Moment of Inertia is defined as ∫y² dA, which results in units of length to the fourth power (m⁴ or mm⁴).

q: 31. M.O.I. of a solid cone about an axis passing through its C.G. and parallel to base is
explain: The formula for the mass moment of inertia of a solid cone about a transverse axis through its CG is (3/20)M(r² + h²/4).

q: 32. M.O.I. of a solid circular cylinder about vertical axis is
explain: A cylinder viewed from the top is a circle; its mass moment of inertia about the central longitudinal axis is the same as a disk: (1/2)Mr².

q: 33. M.O.I. of elliptical section, of major axis = D and minor axis = B, is
explain: For an ellipse with axes B and D, the area MI about the major axis (D) is πBD³/64 (analogous to bd³/12).

q: 34. Polar moment of inertia of a circle (I₀) is given by
explain: The Polar MI (J or Ip) is the sum of Ixx and Iyy. For a circle: πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32.

q: 35. Polar moment of inertia of a rectangle (b x h) is given by
explain: J = Ixx + Iyy = (bh³/12) + (hb³/12) = bh(h² + b²) / 12.

q: 36. Polar moment of inertia of an equilateral triangle of sides x is given by
explain: For an equilateral triangle with side x, Ip = x⁴ / 16√3.

q: 37. Polar moment of inertia is
options: the moment of inertia of an area about an axis parallel to centroidal axis
the moment of an area about an axis which is not lying in the plane of the area
the moment of inertia of an area about a line or axis perpendicular to the plane of the area
explain: By definition, the Polar Moment of Inertia is taken about an axis perpendicular to the cross-section (the Z-axis).

q: 38. The moment of inertia of a triangle (having base = b and height = h) with respect to an axis through the apex and parallel to the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_apex = I_cg + A(d)². d = 2h/3. I_apex = bh³/36 + (1/2 bh)(2h/3)² = bh³/36 + 2bh³/9 = 9bh³/36 = bh³/4.

q: 39. Elasticity of a body is
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the load
the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
large deformability as in case of rubber
explain: Elasticity is the physical property of a material where it returns to its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed.

q: 40. The stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the resistance offered by the material per unit area to a force
explain: Stress is technically the internal resistive force per unit area developed within a body to counteract external loads.

q: 41. A perfectly elastic body is
options: that body which recovers its original shape completely after removal at force
a body of such a material with a lot of extensibility
a body made of rubber only
a body whose cross-sectional dimensions are very small
explain: A perfectly elastic body suffers no permanent deformation; it returns 100% to its original state.

q: 42. Permanent set is
options: the force which acts permanently on the body
the shape of the member just after completion of construction
ratio of Poisson's Ratio to Young's Modulus
explain: When a material is stressed beyond its elastic limit, it retains some deformation even after unloading. This residual deformation is called a permanent set.

q: 43. The Law "Stress is proportional to strain within elastic limits" is formulated by
explain: Hooke's Law states that within the limit of proportionality, stress is directly proportional to strain.

q: 44. A brittle material will
options: never be used for structural purposes
explain: Brittle materials (like cast iron or glass) exhibit very little plastic deformation and fail suddenly by fracture without prior warning (necking).

q: 45. Which of the following is a relatively ductile material?
explain: Mild steel is well known for its high ductility, allowing it to undergo significant plastic deformation (elongation) before failure.

q: 46. By increasing the carbon content in steel, the ultimate tensile strength will
explain: Higher carbon content increases the hardness and tensile strength of steel, although it decreases ductility.

q: 47. With the increase in the carbon content, the ductility of the steel will
explain: As carbon content increases, the steel becomes harder and stronger but more brittle, meaning its ductility decreases.

q: 48. Which of the following materials will have the highest Young's Modulus?
explain: Steel has a Young's Modulus (E) of approximately 200-210 GPa, which is significantly higher than copper (~110 GPa), brass (~100 GPa), or timber (~10 GPa).

q: 49. Creep of a material is
options: continued deformation with time under sustained loading
disappearance of deformation on removal of load
explain: Creep is the slow, progressive permanent deformation of a material under a constant stress over a long period of time.

q: 50. What is tenacity?
explain: Tenacity is the property of a material to resist fracture under tensile stress; it is essentially its ultimate tensile strength.

q: 51. At ordinary temperatures, how is the yield point affected with rate of loading?
explain: At room temperature, the yield strength of most structural metals like mild steel is relatively insensitive to the rate of loading, unlike at high temperatures where strain rate becomes critical.

q: 52. How does the elastic limit vary with increase in temperature?
explain: As temperature increases, the atomic bonds in a material vibrate more vigorously and weaken, leading to a reduction in the stress required to cause permanent deformation (elastic limit).

q: 53. How does the Young's Modulus vary with increase in temperature?
explain: Increased thermal energy increases the interatomic spacing, which decreases the stiffness of the material, thereby reducing the Modulus of Elasticity (E).

q: 54. The moment of resistance developed in a beam subjected to bending moment will, at any instant be
explain: For static equilibrium in a beam, the internal moment of resistance developed by the stresses in the cross-section must exactly balance the external bending moment applied at 그 section.

q: 55. Which of the following materials is suitable for transverse test for modulus of rupture?
explain: The modulus of rupture is commonly determined for brittle or fibrous materials like timber and concrete via a flexure test (transverse loading) to measure their ultimate bending strength.

q: 56. What is the number of basic elements of a force?
explain: A force is characterized by four basic elements: Magnitude, Direction (line of action), Sense (nature), and Point of Application.

q: 57. The property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explain: Elasticity is the ability of a material to deform under load and return to its original dimensions when the load is released.

q: 58. The property of a material by which it can be drawn to smaller section, due to tension, is called
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation under tensile stress, commonly observed when drawing metal into wires.

q: 59. The property of a material by which it can be beaten or rolled into thin plates, is called
explain: Malleability is a material's ability to deform under compressive stress, allowing it to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets without fracturing.

q: 60. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
explain: Once the material surpasses the limit of proportionality and reaches the elastic limit/yield point, the strain increases significantly even with small increases in stress due to plastic flow.

q: 61. The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than that necessary to continue it
explain: In materials like mild steel, there is an Upper Yield Point (to initiate yielding) and a Lower Yield Point (to continue it). The stress to start yielding is higher than the stress required to maintain the yielding process.

q: 62. The phenomenon of slow extension of materials having constant load, i.e. increasing with the time is called
explain: Creep is the time-dependent permanent deformation that occurs when a material is subjected to a constant load for a long duration, especially at elevated temperatures.

q: 63. The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explain: The yielding point is the stage in a stress-strain test where the specimen begins to deform plastically and elongates significantly with little to no increase in the applied load.

q: 64. Every material obeys the Hooke's law within its
explain: Hooke's Law strictly states that stress is proportional to strain only up to the 'Limit of Proportionality'. While the 'Elastic Limit' is close to it, they are technically different points.

q: 65. The materials which have the same elastic properties in all directions, are called
explain: Isotropic materials have identical mechanical properties (like E and G) regardless of the direction in which the property is measured.

q: 66. The law which states, "Within elastic limits strain produced is proportional to the stress producing it", is known as
explain: Hooke's Law is the fundamental principle defining the linear relationship between stress and strain in elastic materials.

q: 67. When equal and opposite forces applied to a body, tend to elongate it, the stress so produced, is called
explain: Tensile stress is the internal resistance developed when external 'pull' forces act to increase the length of a body.

q: 68. The under mentioned type is simple strain
explain: Tensile, compressive, and shear strains are all primary/simple types of deformation corresponding to their respective stress types.

q: 69. A solid cube is subjected to equal normal forces on all its faces. The volumetric strain will be x-times the linear strain in any of the three axes when
explain: Volumetric strain (e_v) for a cube is the sum of linear strains in three mutually perpendicular directions (e_x + e_y + e_z). For equal forces, e_v = 3 * e_linear.

q: 70. The unit of stress in S.I. units is
explain: Stress is force/area. While Pascal ($N/m^2$) is the standard SI unit, multiples and variations like $N/mm^2$ (MPa) are commonly used and valid in SI conventions.

q: 71. The deformation per unit length is called
explain: Strain is the dimensionless measure of deformation, calculated as the change in dimension divided by the original dimension.

q: 72. The unit of strain is
explain: Since strain is the ratio of two lengths (change in length / original length), the units cancel out, making it a dimensionless quantity.

q: 73. Strain is equal to
explain: By definition, strain (ε) is the ratio of change in length (δl) to the original length (l).

q: 74. When a body is subjected to two equal and opposite pulls and as a result the body tends to extend its length, the stress and strain induced is
explain: An external 'pull' results in a tensile internal resistance (stress) and a corresponding elongation (tensile strain).

q: 75. When a body is subjected to two equal and opposite forces, acting tangentially across the resisting section, as a result of which the body tends to shear off across the section, the stress and strain induced is
explain: Tangential forces acting across a section produce shear stress and a resulting angular deformation known as shear strain.

q: 76. Which of the following is a proper sequence?
options: proportional limit, elastic limit, yielding, failure
elastic limit, proportional limit, yielding, failure
explain: In a standard stress-strain curve for mild steel, the material first reaches the limit of proportionality, then the elastic limit, followed by yielding, and finally fracture/failure.

q: 77. Hooke's law holds good up to
explain: While theoretically Hooke's law applies to the limit of proportionality, in many engineering contexts, it is considered valid up to the elastic limit where the linear relationship is mostly maintained.

q: 78. Whenever a material is loaded within elastic limit, stress is ................ strain.
explain: This is the core definition of Hooke's Law: within the elastic range, stress varies linearly with strain.

q: 79. The ratio of linear stress to the linear strain is called
explain: Young's Modulus, or the Modulus of Elasticity (E), is the constant ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.

q: 80. The unit of modulus of elasticity is same as those of
options: stress, force and modulus of rigidity
stress, pressure and modulus of rigidity
explain: Since strain is dimensionless, the modulus of elasticity (stress/strain) has the same units as stress, pressure, and modulus of rigidity ($N/m^2$ or Pascal).

q: 81. When a change in length takes place, the strain is known as
explain: Linear strain (or longitudinal strain) refers to the deformation occurring along the axis of the applied force.

q: 82. The change in length due to a tensile or compressive force acting on a body is given by
explain: From $\sigma = E \epsilon$, we get $P/A = E(\delta l/l)$. Rearranging for change in length gives $\delta l = Pl/AE$.

q: 83. The modulus of elasticity for mild steel is approximately equal to
explain: The standard value of Young's Modulus for steel is around $2 	imes 10^5 	ext{ N/mm}^2$ (or 200-210 GPa).

q: 84. Young's modulus may be defined as the ratio of
explain: Young's Modulus (E) defines the stiffness of a material under axial loading (linear stress/linear strain).

q: 85. Modulus of rigidity may be defined as the ratio of
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (G or C) is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain, representing the material's resistance to shearing deformation.

q: 86. Two bars of different materials and same size are subjected to same tensile force. If the bars have unit elongation in the ratio of 2:5, then the ratio of modulus of elasticity of the two materials will be
explain: Since $\delta l = Pl/AE$, and P, l, A are constant, $E$ is inversely proportional to elongation. Thus, $E_1/E_2 = \delta l_2/\delta l_1 = 5/2$.

q: 87. When a bar of length l and diameter d is rigidly fixed at upper end and hanging freely, then total elongation produced in the bar due to its own weight is
explain: The elongation of a prismatic bar due to its own weight is given by $\delta l = \gamma l^2 / 2E$, where $\gamma$ (or w) is weight per unit volume.

q: 88. The deformation of a bar under its own weight is ................ the deformation, if the same body is subjected to a direct load equal to the weight of the body.
explain: Deformation under own weight is $WL/2AE$, while deformation under external load W is $WL/AE$. Therefore, self-weight causes half the deformation.

q: 89. The elongation of a conical bar under its own weight is ................ that of a prismatic bar of same length.
explain: The elongation of a conical bar due to self-weight is $\gamma l^2 / 6E$, which is exactly $1/3$ of the prismatic bar's elongation ($\gamma l^2 / 2E$).

q: 90. The length of a conical bar is l, density w and modulus of elasticity E. The elongation of the bar under the action of its own weight will be
explain: As derived in mechanics, the self-weight elongation of a cone is $\frac{wl^2}{6E}$.

q: 91. Strain rosters are used to
explain: Strain rosettes are a combination of three or more strain gauges used to measure the linear strains in different directions on a surface to determine the state of strain at a point.

q: 92. The extension of a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 to d2 is length l and subjected to an axial pull P is
explain: For a tapering bar, the effective area is replaced by the geometric mean of the end areas, resulting in the formula $\delta l = \frac{4Pl}{\pi E d_1 d_2}$.

q: 93. The maximum stress produced in a bar of tapering section is at
explain: Since Stress = Force / Area, for a constant axial force, the stress is maximum where the cross-sectional area is minimum (the smaller end).

q: 94. Modular ratio of the two materials is the ratio of
explain: The modular ratio ($m$) is defined as the ratio of the Modulus of Elasticity of one material to another ($E_1/E_2$), often used in composite section analysis.

q: 95. The shear modulus of most materials with respect to the modulus of elasticity is
explain: From $G = E / 2(1+\mu)$, since $\mu$ (Poisson's ratio) is usually between 0.25 and 0.33 for metals, $G$ is typically around $0.37E$ to $0.4E$, which is less than half.

q: 96. A rod is enclosed centrally in a tube and the assembly is subjected to a compressive load, then
options: both rod and tube are under compression
tube is under tension and rod is under compression
explain: In a composite assembly subjected to an external compressive load, both components must compress together to maintain compatibility of displacement.

q: 97. When a bar is subjected to a change of temperature and its deformation is prevented, the stress induced in the bar is
explain: Thermal stress is induced in a body when its free expansion or contraction due to temperature change is restricted by external supports.

q: 98. A steel bar 5 m long and 40 mm wide is heated from 15°C to 40°C and it is free to expand. The bar will induce
explain: If a material is free to expand or contract during a temperature change without any restraint, no internal resistance (stress) is developed.

q: 99. When a bar is cooled to -5°C, it will develop
explain: Cooling causes a material to contract. If this contraction is prevented, the material 'tries' to pull away from the supports, inducing tensile stress.

q: 100. A bar of copper and steel form a composite system, which is heated to a temperature of 40°C. The stress induced in the copper bar will be
explain: Copper has a higher coefficient of thermal expansion than steel. When heated, copper wants to expand more but is restricted by the steel, putting copper into compression and steel into tension.
